claims.text: Under simultaneous mechanical loading and corrosive exposure, high-entropy alloys maintain a dynamically self-renewing, defect-tolerant passive layer.
This passive layer substantially reduces localized corrosion under simultaneous wear and corrosion.
This passive layer substantially reduces wear under simultaneous wear and corrosion.
Hard oxide or nitride films form and repair rapidly at mechanical contact sites.
NbMoTaTi-based high-entropy alloys have a reported capacity for passivation.
Laser-cladded high-entropy-alloy microstructures can combine high hardness with passive-film-based corrosion resistance.
The proposed comparison uses simultaneous sliding contact, electrochemical monitoring, and in situ AFM or confocal imaging in chloride solution.
The proposed test operates at 5–10 cm/s, 5–10 N, 0.6–3.5 wt.% NaCl, room temperature, and up to two hours.
The protective surface layer is continuously formed, mechanically disrupted, and reformed during tribocorrosion.
Multi-principal-element-induced lattice distortion contributes to surface hardening.
Strong oxide- or nitride-forming tendencies produce robust passivation.
Rapid repassivation after mechanical disruption prevents deeper damage and diminishes wear–corrosion synergy.
Relative to stainless steel, the high-entropy alloy will have at least 20–40% lower wear-volume loss during combined wear and corrosion.
Relative to stainless steel, the high-entropy alloy will have a lower friction coefficient during combined wear and corrosion.
Relative to stainless steel, the high-entropy alloy will have up to an order-of-magnitude lower corrosion current density during combined wear and corrosion.
Real-time imaging will reveal repetitive passive-layer disruption followed by rapid regrowth, with damage confined to shallow, sporadic sites.
Stainless steel will show greater total wear loss, more pitting, and higher corrosion current because its disrupted passive film heals more slowly.
At very high loads or in extremely acidic or high-chloride environments, passive-film repair may not keep pace with mechanical damage and the protective effect will decline.
Composition and loading-rate variations may alter passivation dynamics, so the proposed mechanism may not apply to every high-entropy alloy.
Absence of visible rapid film reformation together with no significant reduction in wear–corrosion synergy relative to stainless steel would falsify the hypothesis.
